title: The Spilled Coffee That Made Him Likable
text:
In 1966 Elliot Aronson, Ben Willerman and Joanne Floyd asked male students at the University of Minnesota to listen to a tape recording of a candidate trying out for the College Bowl, a televised quiz contest. Students were told they would rate how much they liked him.

There were four versions of the tape. In two, the candidate was nearly perfect, answering almost every question correctly and mentioning impressive achievements in school. In the other two, he was mediocre, getting only about a third right and describing an ordinary record. Near the end of one tape of each kind, there was a clatter, the sound of a cup falling, and the candidate exclaiming that he had spilled coffee all over his new suit.

The results were neat. The superior candidate who spilled the coffee was rated the most attractive of all, liked more than the same superior candidate without the accident. The mediocre candidate who spilled coffee was rated least attractive. A blunder, it seemed, made an impressive person more human and approachable, while it only made an unimpressive person look worse. Later studies found the effect depends on the observer as well, and is strongest among people of average self-esteem.
lesson: If people already see you as competent, admitting small mistakes makes you easier to like. Polished perfection can keep others at a distance.
people: Elliot Aronson, Ben Willerman, Joanne Floyd
source: Aronson, E., Willerman, B., and Floyd, J. (1966). The effect of a pratfall on increasing interpersonal attractiveness. Psychonomic Science, 4(6), 227-228.
